label: Person
name: Adam Kozłowiecki
summary:
Adam Kozłowiecki (1911–2007) was a Polish Jesuit cardinal who survived Dachau concentration camp to become the founding Archbishop of Lusaka and one of the most celebrated missionaries of twentieth-century Africa. Born in Huta Komorowska, he entered the Jesuits and was studying theology in Kraków when the Nazis arrested him in November 1939, sending him to Sachsenhausen and then Dachau, where he remained until liberation in April 1945.

After his release, Kozłowiecki joined the Jesuit mission in Northern Rhodesia (later Zambia), where he worked from 1946 until the end of his active ministry. He was appointed the first Archbishop of Lusaka in 1959 and served until 1969, overseeing the Church's transition through Zambian independence in 1964. He then continued as a simple parish priest in rural Zambia—the longest-serving foreign priest in the country's history—refusing elevation and comfort in favour of direct pastoral service. Pope John Paul II created him cardinal in pectore in 1998, publicly revealing the appointment the following year.

Kozłowiecki's life trajectory—from Dachau to Lusaka's archbishop to village priest—made him an icon of radical Christian service. He spent sixty years in Zambia and died there in 2007. His memoir of Dachau and his reflections on Africa became important documents of both the Holocaust's Catholic victims and the postcolonial African Church.

Jesuit missionary strategy in British Central Africa identified Northern Rhodesia as a priority evangelisation territory

His sixty-year presence in Zambia created lasting bonds between Polish Catholicism and the Zambian Church
His cardinalate gave visibility to both Holocaust Catholic survivors and African mission work
